families.zh: 潘治的娜娜夫人 · 方孔铜钱

specimens.title: S#1589, Central Asia, Turgesh, cash-like coin, m/a
specimens.description: Thick and heavy specimen. Compare with Z# 33694 , 189825 , 189826 and 189860 . Metal composition is : Cu 89.1810, Zn 0.3187, Sn 3.7445, As 0.7834, Sb 0.9928, Pb 2.7717, Fe 0.1788, Mn 1.7085, Ni 0.3105, Cd,Co,Bi all are under detection limits, Sum 99.9899 %, XRF data. So we see As-Sb bearing, low led and low tin bronze. Manganese content may be connected with attempts of previous owner to darken the coin with using of KMnO4+CuSO4 solution. Patination is sulphide type - in some points sulphur content reach up to 3 %.

specimens.title: S#1589, Central Asia, Turgesh, cash-like coin, m/a
specimens.description: Compare with Z# 33693 , 189825 , 189826 and 189860 . Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 55.7065, Sn 4.1952, As 2.2783, Pb 36.7685, Fe 0.8302, Ni 0.1179, Zn,Sb,Cd,Bi,Co,Mn all are under detection and error limits, Sum 99.8966%, XRF data. Metal colour and composition are strong different from #33693. Zinc and stibium absent here, lead and tin contents elevated, copper content is lower more than 1/3. Apparently alloy is heterogeneous (liquated). Patination of the coin is phosphate type (up to 2.8 % P) and presumably represented by pyromorphite Pb5[PO4]3Cl. We can suppose, that this coin was made on another mint that Z# 33693 .

specimens.title: Sogdiana, bronze cash-like coin, ikshid Turgar 738-750 A.D., m/a
specimens.description: Close to #5464 and #16056, but almost twice more lightweight. Also some difference in obverse/reverse orientation exist. On the image #5464 inaccuracy present - side with crescent is turned on 180 degree clockwise. But on this specimen we have exactly such orientation as on image of #5464. Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 88.9227, Zn 0.5745, Sn 6.1167, Sb 0.5930, Pb 2.3025, Fe 0.4925, Ni 0.3465, As,Bi,Cd,Co all are under detection or error levels, Sum 99.3484 %, XRF data. So we have here low-tin and low-lead bronze. More local microprobe analysis gave composition in a point: Cu 93.91, Zn 0.0, Sn 4.87, Sb 0.26, Pb 0.0, Fe 0.52, Sum 99.56 % microprobe data. Compare with Z# 48603 .

specimens.title: Samarqand, AE, Turgar.
specimens.description: Ex Stephen Album rare coins: Auction 7: Lot 95 SOGDIANA: Turghar, Ikhshid, 740-760, AE cash (2.65g), Samarkand. Smirnova-519 type II. Sogdian legend around central square hole / Tamghas around central square hole, with crescent at reverse top. The Sogdian states, although never politically united, were centered around the main city of Samarkand. Sogdiana lay north of Bactria, east of Khwarezm, and southeast of Kangju between the Oxus (Amu Darya) and the Jaxartes (Syr Darya), embracing the fertile valley of the Zarafshan (the ancient Polytimetus). Sogdian territory corresponds to the provinces of Samarkand and Bokhara in modern Uzbekistan as well as the Sughd province of modern Tajikistan. Dates of rulers reigns are still not completely certain.

specimens.title: Sogdiana AE cash, Kai-yuan tong-bao, rev. tamgha and Sogdian word
specimens.description: Unearthed in Kyrgyzstan. Coins of this type are listed at Smirnova, O. I. “Svodnyi katalog sogdiiskikh monet. Bronza” [General catalogue of Sogdian coins. Bronze]. Moscow, 1981, p.p. 101-102, 403( Table III, ##43-47); Smirnova, O. I. "Catalogue of Coins from the Settlement Penjikent", p. 177 (Table IV, #29). DH # 14.17 type. “Rev: Sogdian legend, possibly Bugh (Lord or God), which could refer to a deity, the Chinese Emperor, or the Turkish Qagan. These imitations of Kai Yuans were issued in the Sogd area (present day Uzbekistan) during the 7th century. The petty kings of the area had established diplomatic relations with the Chinese”. Compare with # # 37290 , 6283 . Unusual die axis. Samarqand tamgha (another version: Chinese key 刀 "dao" ("Knife"), stylized as a Y-shaped tamgha of Ishkhids of Sogdiana) (top) and Soghdian word "βgy" (baga) = ruler, God or Lord (bottom) on reverse. Coins with such type of Tamgha's orientation were not listed in Smirnova.

specimens.title: Western Liao, zhou yuan tong bao
specimens.description: Original description by Laosa: Kai-yuan Tong-bao, strange calligraphic variety. This is a Central Asian imitation of Tang Dynasty square-holed coins with the legend ‘Kai-yuan Tong-bao’ (開元通寶). Another possible reading is 周元通寶 [Zhou-yuan tong bao]. Unearthed on the territory of Kyrgyzstan. Image source: www.amurklad.org Character 開 [kai] is written with the radical similar to 口 instead of 井 between the “doors” (門), it also resembles the character 周, but I suppose it must be a degraded character 開 [kai]. Character 元 [yuan] below the hole is written in a strange archaic script and has both ‘left and right shoulders’ (左右挑双挑元). The similar coin unearthed in the same area can be seen there: Zeno # 172880 . Also compare to Zeno ## 162023 and 162024 .

specimens.description: Smirnova #657 Obv: Sogdian legend MLK WRK WRTRMWK (king Urk Wartarmuka) Rev: tamgha of Samarkand (left) and the triskele tamgha of the kings dynasty (right) Compare with Z# 123439 . Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 70.36, Sn 12.83, As 1.23, Sb 0.61, Pb 14.85, Zn,Bi,Fe,Co,Ni are under detection or error limits, Sum 99.84 %, microprobe data in scanning mode on 90x20 mkm surface. The alloy is binary and composed by groundmass of composition Cu 81.97, Sn 12.85, As 1.72, Sb 0.81, Pb 2.26, Ni 0.23, Sum 99.84 % with abundant inclusions of composition Sn 6.53, Pb 93.43, Sum 99.96 % (point microprobe data). So we have here nonmagnetic Sb-As-bearing tin lead bronze.

specimens.title: Soghd, bronze cash, principality Samitan, Nanaiabiat Samidanian, m/a
specimens.description: Obv: Sogdian legend around square hole nny'βy't smyδ'nč, which can be translated as 'Nanaiabiat Samidanian', Samidan being the town's name, Nanaiabiat the ruler. Rev: Tamgha each side of square hole. The identical tamghas are in the form of a semi-circle on a pedestal; small annulet in semi-circle. Ref.: Fedorov, M., & Kuznetsov, A. (2010). A Rare Sogdian Coin from the Ming Tepe Hillfort. British Institute of Persian Studies, 48, 163-165. Fedorov, M., & Kuznetsov, A. (2010). A Hoard of Early Medieval Sogdian Bronze Coins from the Ming Tepe Hillfort. The Numismatic Chronicle, 170, 446-451. Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 46.23, Sn 10.44, Pb 41.22, Fe 1.50, Zn,As,Sb,Bi,Co,Ni are under detection or error limits, Sum 99.39 %, microprobe data in scanning mode on 120x100 mkm surface. The alloy is binary and composed by groundmass of composition Cu 90.28, Sn 7.39, As 0.72, Pb 0.57, Fe 0.82, Sum 99.78 % with abundant inclusions of pure lead (point microprobe data). So we have here magnetic yellow iron-bearing high-lead tin bronze.

From a small group recently offered on the market. The 4th example sold in Stephen Album Auction 20, Lot 87, for $500.

specimens.title: Tutuks, AE
specimens.description: From my personal collection, I bought this around 2018 or so off of eBay. What is the correct attribution for this series of 'ash' runic square hole coins? Smirnova #1445. This type is attributed to Ferghana by Hartill in his GCC, #4.28, as well as by Michael Fedorov in his 2003 article "Money circulation in early-mediaeval Ustrushana, Farghana, and Tokharistan (6th - first half of 8th century AD)". Smirnova does not attribute it (to my limited knowledge) but she includes the findspots of Kuva, Ferghana, one from Bukhara, and three from Otrar. Smirnova also points out that this type had not been found Semirech'e. What is the reason for attributing it to Sayram here on Zeno? Is there more recent evidence that points to this? Fedorov suggests that the city of Osh in present-day Uzbekistan may be the meaning of the "Ash" or "Ush" runic letter. Is there any other evidence or theories? I wrote a thread about this coin on CoinTalk in 2019. It is mostly speculation and I did not really understand the series, nor the context for these Central Asian cash imitations, so I am sure that it is riddled with inaccuracies. At the time I was using Hartill and Smirnova's works and I landed on a conclusion of Ferghana, 627-649, by a local Göktürk ruler possibly named Kan Bagatur. This coin measures 16mm long (with sprue), 15mm wide, and 1mm thick. Obv: Runic letter "ush" right, surrounding " 'lpw y'y'n twtwy" Rev: Blank (uniface)

specimens.title: Yaghlaqar clan AE, Unknown ruler.
specimens.description: Ex Stephen Album Rare Coins Auction 49 13-16 June 2024, lot 79. Starting price: 350 USD YAGHLAQAR CLAN: Unknown ruler, late 8th century, AE cash, type #1 (4.06g), Kamyshev-34/35, Zeno-46641, Soghdian or Uighur legends on both sides, with the Yaghlaqar tamgha on the obverse, the word left of the tamgha is possibly the name of the ruler, but remains undeciphered; this piece is of finer condition than the 9 pieces posted on Zeno and the first to be offered at auction anywhere, excellent VF. Although the Yaghlaqar clan had been in the Turfan area of Xinjiang, China, they were forced west late in the 8th century. The coins are found around Krasnaya Rechka of Kyrgyzstan, in the Chuy Valley east of Bishkek and close to the border with Kazakhstan. There are two variants, types #1 and #2, which differ only in the form of the Yaghlaqar toughra, as noted on Zeno. Price realized: 650 USD

specimens.title: Western Liao, zhou yuan tong bao. Rev. large dot
specimens.description: Listed at SARC Premier Auctions Auction 53, September18-21, 2025 WESTERN LIAO: Uncertain Ruler, ca. 12th century, AE cash (4.50g), Zeno-330709, zhou yuan tong bao imitating the Later Zhou Dynasty issue in expressive and wild calligraphy, large dot below on reverse, graded 80 by GBCA Grading Company and misattributed on the holder, VF $1,500 - 2,500 This is the second example of this rare type we have handled. See Belyaev & Sidorovich (2023) for an in-depth discussion on this series (“Apropos of the coins with the legend zhou-yuan tong-bao from the finds in Kyrgyzstan” in Revue de la Société de Numismatique Asiatique, vol. 47, pp. 37-44), as well as Zeno for an overview of published articles on Western Liao coinage (www.zeno.ru/showgallery.php?cat=9299).

specimens.title: China, Western Liao, Malik Aram Yinal Qaraj مالك ارام ىىنال قرج, heavy, m/a
specimens.description: Proto-Qarakhanid, Semirech'ye bronze cash Heavy unworked specimen with hole filled with metal. Compare with Z# 228047 , 228228 , 236091 , 236371 , 256454 and 281281 . Note that their bronzes are different colours. Obv.: Malik Aram Yinal Chig (in Arab.) t-r-b-l Rev.: plain Metal composition of the coin is: Cu 78.41, Zn 7.29, Sn 11.32, As 0.35, Sb 1.16, Pb 0.85, Fe 0.33, Ni 0.18, Co below error level, Sum 99.90%, microprobe data in scanning mode on surface 30x20 mkm. So we have here very low-lead, zincian bronze of yellow colour. Atomic ratio Zn+Fe:Sn ~ 1:1 of the alloy is close to one in mineral kesterite ( https://www.mindat.org/min-2189.html ). Ores with kesterite could to be mined in Zeravshan or Inylchek ranges in Kyrgyzstan. Degradation of the alloy during alteration in ground is typical for bronzes. Leaching of Zn from the coins surface resulted not in redcashization (formation of red copper outer layer) typical for brasses, but silvery-white film of intermetallide Cu2Sn (well visible along the coin edge) was formed. Mineralization crust of the coin is oxide-carbonate type (tenorite + minium -> hydroromarchite -> cerussite) tell us, that the coin initially was burned in open flame and later was oxidized not deep in ground in cold fresh ground water.

specimens.title: Kai-yuan Tong-bao, strange calligraphic variety, unlisted
specimens.description: This is a Central Asian imitation of Tang Dynasty square-holed coins with the legend ‘Kai-yuan Tong-bao’ (開元通寶). Unearthed in Chuy (Chui) region, Kyrgyzstan. Character 開 [kai] is written in ‘running’ script. For me it resembles the character 关 (関) [guan], but it is only my guess. The top element of character 寶 [bao] resembles the radical 山 [shan] – ‘mountain’. Element 貝 [bei] of character 寶 features several separated dots (with lines between them). Probably, this is a pictographic character representing the local landscape – mountains, stones and rivers. I invented a special Chinese term for this calligraphic variety: 山冠点贝宝 – “Character ‘bao’ with radical ‘shan’ on top and dots in radical ‘bei’.” The similar coin unearthed in the same area can be seen there: Zeno # 162023 .

specimens.title: Da Li Yuan Bao from Kyrgyzstan, m/a
specimens.description: The coin was unearthed at Krasnorechenskoe site (Kyrgyzstan), and apparently is local imitation of such coins issued in Xinjiang in Tang times. Compare with Z##696 and 697. These coins has distinctly yellow colour metal different from one of original Xinjiang issues. Compare also with Z# 223061 . Composition of metal of the coin also is uncommon: Cu 70.28, Sn 20.01, As 1.96, Pb 7.11, Fe 0.47, Ag,Zn,Sb,Bi,Co,Ni all are below detection or error levels, Sum 99.83%, microprobe data in scanning mode on surface 250x150 mkm. So we have here yellow As-bearing high-tin, low-lead bronze very different from usual for Xinjiang issues (cf. Z## 37794 , 44241 , 158424 and 172899 ) high-lead, moderately tin pinkish bronzes. Structure of this bronze also is very unusual and enigmatic for me - it is homogeneous on back-scattered electron images being heterogeneous compositionally. Point microprobe analysa gave wide deviations of main components Cu 85.22-74.32, Sn 11.54-15.54, As 1.25-2.32, Pb 0.00-7.44. But high-tin compositions (giving elevated tin content to alloy) weren't found. Besides that alloy don't contains desseminated pure lead drops so typical for Chinese lead bronzes structure. By other words the alloy was melted under very high temperatures and had cool very fast, what implys very different casting technology. Besides that the alloy is enriched with silver. Instead of lead drops it contains small (2-15 mkm) but abundant inclusions of pure silver. They are present not in metal itself, but in products of its alteration. This means, that the bronze contains silver in concentrations below sensitivity of microprobe 0.20% (only one point analysis gave 1.57% Ag), but during oxidation of base metals silver detached from alloy, concentrated and form its own phase. So we may conclude, that such coins are local Middle Asian production, imitations of Chinese Da Li YB, were cast by original technology from local raw materials. Mineralization of the coin now (after elimination of main copper mineralization) is represented by grey films of lead (carbonates, oxychlorides) and tin (hydroromarchite) minerals.

specimens.title: Da Li Yuan Bao from Kyrgyzstan, m/a
specimens.description: The coin was unearthed in Kyrgyzstan, and obviously is local imitation of such coins issued in Xinjiang in Tang times. Composition of the coin alloy is: Cu 85.11/86.47, Sn 11.79/11.17, As 1.03/1.49, Sb 0.39/0.32, Pb 1.25/0.00, Fe 0.25/0.22, Co 0.00/0.12, Ni 0.18/0.21, Zn is below detection level, Sum 100.00/100.00 %, microprobe data in scanning mode on 2000x1200/1200x250 mkm surface. Point analysis is Cu 88.26, Sn 9.81, As 1.09, Sb 0.34, Fe 0.15, Co 0.08, Ni 0.13, Zn and Pb are below detection level, Sum 99.86 %. So the coin was cast of homogeneous tin, low-lead, yellow, nonmagnetic bronze. Compare with Z# 134419 , 223061 and 232134 .

specimens.title: Semirech'e, AE cash, rev. 4 tamghas. Unpublished.
specimens.description: Personal collection item, so far an unique specimen. The excavation point of the coin is unknown as it was mixed with a hoard of dirhams from many time periods when being sold. This was the only early Medieval Semirech'e styled coinage in the mix. In my personal belief there are two main possibilities for the tamgha: one is that it is closely related to the wine-glass tamgha settlers in the 9th century, before the area's coinage was fully controlled by the Kara Khanids. Reason for this belief is that the wine-glass tamgha, when bottom part removed, becomes the current tamgha. Research by Babayarov 2019 presented at the Inner Mongolia University conference show that details are added to Turkic tamghas as local rulers seek to delineate their own rulership from that of the central khaganate or from other rulers. The similarity of this tamgha to ram horns from the Afrasiab murals is astonishing, possibly suggesting a Turkic connection. Krasnaya Rechka and Suyab are two locations that seem possible for the original casting of this coin, for the first has unearthed the wine glass tamgha coins and the latter has been the capital for the Western Turks, the Turgesh, and the Karluks, three main coin casters of Semirech'e known to cast in this style. A second possibility is that this coin's tamghas evolved from the Chinese character "元", which could be a result of Sino-Turko iconographic fusion. There is evidence that the character "元" has appeared on Turgesh coins from the Black Turgesh faction casted by ruler W'xswt'wy (recent research by numismatist Wu Zhonghua in his book "Turgesh Coinage" suggest that Turgesh coins were factionalized between Black and Yellow tribes, and that the Black tribe uses the runic tamgha while the Yellow uses the "X" tamgha). It is plausible that the character became a tamgha, though this in my personal belief is the less possible explanation. Given the effaced nature of the coin's obverse it is unclear who the issuers were. The late 9th century Arslanids have casted coinage with a reverse that has four tamghas, presented in Kamyshev 2002, and the tamghas also have possible ram horn elements. The connection is unclear, but the weight and design of both types of coinage is extremely similar.

specimens.title: Aniepigraphic Turgesh cash (8th c. AD) with imprint of Samanid dirham (279-289 AH), found in Chach
specimens.description: Shinji Hirano, "A Semerich'e Hoard Allegedly from Chach" in Zeno Festschrift 20th Anniversary, 2024. https://zeno.ru/data3/Festschrift/Shinji%20Hirano%20-%20A%20Semirech'e%20coin%20hoard%20allegedly%20from%20Chach.pdf " One coin bears the imprinted in patina part of the reverse die of a silver Samanid dirham, probably due the contact with the coin in the earth, although the Samanid dirham itself was not presented in this hoard (Fig. 2, No. 70). Visible mirror part of the dirham’s field legend allows to attribute coin to Isma’il b. Ahmad (279‒295 AH). In the legend is also cited caliph al-Mutadid, which allows to narrow period of coin issue to 279‒289 AH / 892‒903 AD (see for example dirham Z‒287961). "
